_readme: Set 114 Session 3 — the cross-language parity corpus for the step
checklist's row builder.
Session 3 renders an in-flight session's steps in the Work Explorer.
The Explorer is TypeScript, the checklist is Python, and Set 114 S2's
routed ai-assignment.md is explicit about the one acceptable way to
bridge them: 'port the rule with a shared fixture that proves the two
agree row-for-row'. This is that fixture.
TWO suites assert against it, and neither one owns it:
ai_router/tests/test_step_row_parity.py
writes each case to a tmpdir and drives the real
session_checklist.build_rows / read_spec_steps.
tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/src/test/suite/sessionStepModel.test.ts
drives providers/sessionStepModel.ts's buildStepRows /
parseSpecSteps over the same inputs.
So: change Python alone and the Python test fails. Change TypeScript
alone and the TypeScript test fails. Change this file alone and BOTH
fail. There is no edit that silently diverges the two.
expectedRows is the RENDERED row list in order. expectedSpecSteps is
what spec.md declares for that session, which decides only whether
ordinal reconciliation is trustworthy — it never contributes a row.
ONE DECLARED DIVERGENCE (Set 120 Session 3, operator ruling
2026-08-11). The '<- here' marker was removed from Python:
session_checklist.HERE_MARKER, its two rendering sites, _mark_here
and ChecklistRow.is_here are all gone, because the in-progress status
token now carries that fact directly and the marker's single-valued
design is what made it point confidently at the wrong row when the
data was bad. The EXTENSION keeps its markHere until the extension
carve deletes that derivation wholesale (Set 120 standing decision 3:
no extension changes in this set).
So 'isHere' below is now pinned for the TYPESCRIPT half only.
test_step_row_parity.py compares on the five fields both
implementations still produce (stepNumber, stepKey, description,
status, isPlanned) and projects isHere out of the expectation;
sessionStepModel.test.ts is unchanged and still asserts it. Do NOT
strip isHere from these cases as a cleanup — it is the only coverage
the extension's marker has, and test_the_corpus_still_pins_the
_extensions_here_marker fails if it goes.

cases.why: The common case. cases.name: identity-beats-ordinal
cases.why: A logged step whose stepKey EQUALS a planned key claims that row even though its stepNumber points elsewhere. A key match asserts identity and cannot be wrong; an ordinal match is an inference. Round 2 of Set 114 S2's verification is why the passes are in this order.

cases.name: plan-moved-under-the-session
cases.why: THE PLANTED DEFECT (L-112-1). The spec gained a step after registration, so the seeded plan no longer matches spec.md and the ordinal pass is switched OFF. With it on, the inserted step would claim the old step 2's row, that step would claim step 3's, and the LAST planned row would vanish — a planned step nobody executed, silently dropped. Here every planned row survives and the logged step appends.

cases.name: bookkeeping-cannot-claim-a-planned-row
cases.why: An entry carrying a `kind` is machinery's record ABOUT the session — several are written at registration, before any work exists. It RENDERS (it is part of the record and Set 111 S4 showed it) but it may not mark a planned step done. Without this rule a set with pathAwareCritique configured would show step 1 as complete before the session started.

cases.name: repeated-key-collapses-to-the-latest-at-the-first-position
cases.why: activity-log.json is append-only, so a step logged in-progress and later complete appears twice. Rendering both duplicates the row AND strands the marker on the stale entry. The collapse keeps the LATEST entry at the position the step FIRST appeared.

cases.name: anonymous-steps-are-not-collapsed
cases.why: Steps logged with no stepKey cannot be collapsed: two anonymous steps are two steps, not one shown twice.

cases.name: everything-finished-marks-the-last-row
cases.why: With no unfinished row anywhere the marker falls to the last one, so the checklist never renders without a 'here'.

cases.name: planned-row-takes-the-marker-only-when-no-logged-step-is-unfinished
cases.why: The marker prefers the first unfinished LOGGED step over an earlier still-pending PLANNED one. Without that ordering, a session on step 3 whose planned step 2 was never claimed would point the operator at step 2 — the 'where is this session' question answered wrongly.

cases.name: a-falsy-non-string-kind-is-no-kind-at-all
cases.why: THE PATH-AWARE CRITIQUE'S CATCH (gpt-5.5, Set 114 S3). `kind` is untrusted on-disk data, and Python reads it with `str(x or "")` -- so `0` and `false` are 'no kind', i.e. an ORDINARY LOGGED STEP that may claim a planned row. The TypeScript mirror originally used `String(x ?? "")`, which falls back only on null/undefined and turned those into the literal strings "0" and "false" -- bookkeeping, forbidden from claiming. The two surfaces then disagreed about which row was current and whether a planned step had been executed. No shipping writer emits this, which is exactly why only a second reading lens found it and why it belongs here now: the corpus is what stops it reopening.

cases.name: falsy-non-string-fields-read-as-empty
cases.why: The same coercion class as the case above, on the other string-ish fields. Python's `str(x or "")` turns a falsy non-string `stepKey` / `description` / `status` into the empty string, so such a step is ANONYMOUS (uncollapsible -- two of them are two rows) and its status is unknown rather than the literal text "0". A mirror using `??` would render "0" as a label and as a status token, and would collapse the two rows into one.

cases.why: The Work Explorer's required degradation: no rows means no children, never a stale or invented list.
